analysis.one_liner: Sets patient protections in HMO and health insurance plans, including emergency care, specialist access, appeals, and the right to sue.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a vote: after referral to two House committees and their subcommittees in early 1999, no action followed before the 106th Congress ended in January 2001.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have written a set of patient protections into federal law for everyone in managed care plans or health insurance. Plans would have to cover emergency room visits without prior approval, let patients see specialists and OB-GYNs without gatekeeper referrals, disclose what they cover and how they pay doctors, run fair and timely reviews of denials, and offer appeals to outside reviewers. It would also have opened the door for patients to sue their health plan under state law when careless plan decisions cause injury or death. The bill sat in committee and never came up for a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: The roughly 160 million Americans covered by employer plans and private insurance at the time, especially people in HMO-style plans with gatekeeper rules: anyone needing emergency care, specialist care, ongoing treatment, or a fair appeal of a coverage denial. It also protects doctors from plan gag clauses and from being scapegoated for the plan's decisions, and creates independent health insurance ombudsmen to help consumers.

how_it_helps.text: Plans must cover emergency services without prior authorization and cannot bill patients more for using an out-of-network emergency room, using a 'prudent layperson' standard for what counts as an emergency

Patients get direct access to OB-GYN and pediatric care, referrals to specialists for serious conditions, standing referrals for ongoing conditions, and continuity of care when a provider leaves the network — including through pregnancy and terminal illness

Plans must run utilization review under written criteria without financial incentives tied to denying care, decide prior authorizations within 3 business days and continued-care decisions within 1 day, and give written reasons for denials

Patients get internal appeals with expedited 72-hour review and an independent external appeal whose decision binds the plan; denials worth more than $100 or that jeopardize health are appealable externally

Contracts that gag doctors from discussing treatment options with patients, or that make doctors indemnify the plan for the plan's own mistakes, are void; plans cannot operate physician incentive plans that reward inappropriate denials

Plans must cover routine patient costs for people with serious illnesses joining federally approved clinical trials, must meet network adequacy standards, and must disclose benefits, cost-sharing, formulary restrictions, and physician compensation incentives

The bill amends ERISA so that patients can sue HMOs and insurers under state law for personal injury or wrongful death caused by careless plan decisions, a right largely blocked by federal preemption at the time
States receive grants to run independent health insurance ombudsmen to counsel consumers choosing coverage and fighting denials

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers and HMOs bear the cost: new coverage mandates, staffing for regulated utilization review, external appeal costs paid by the plan, disclosure and ombudsman obligations, and exposure to state-law damage suits. Employers may face some administrative and premium costs, though the bill largely shields employers from the new lawsuits and requires no employer payments for the point-of-service option. Some of the added cost would flow to consumers through premiums.

drawbacks.text: The new mandates and liability exposure would raise administrative costs, and those costs would show up partly in premiums; the bill itself allows plans to charge higher premiums and cost-sharing for the point-of-service out-of-network option

Opening plans to state-law damage suits could increase litigation and drive up coverage costs, which is why employer groups historically opposed this provision even though the bill shields employers themselves from most such suits

Several protections are options rather than free benefits: the point-of-service choice can carry extra cost-sharing, and the bill does not require plans to cover services they exclude or guarantee the availability of any particular provider

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill addressed well-documented problems of 1990s managed care — surprise emergency bills, gatekeepers blocking specialists, secret denial criteria, gag clauses, and patients left without recourse when plans made bad calls. The main honest cost is higher premiums from mandates and liability exposure, which could nudge some employers toward dropping coverage; the bill's drafters partially blunted that by shielding employers from most lawsuits and letting consumers pay extra for out-of-network choice. On balance the protections were substantial and the cost was diffuse.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to two House committees and their subcommittees in early 1999 and sat there with no markup, no committee vote, and no floor vote for the rest of the Congress.

narrative.text: Rep. Greg Ganske, a Republican physician from Iowa, introduced the Managed Care Reform Act on February 11, 1999, with 17 cosponsors (14 Republicans, 3 Democrats)
The Speaker referred the bill to the Commerce Committee and, in addition, to the Education and the Workforce Committee, splitting jurisdiction between them
In March 1999 the bill was referred to the Commerce Subcommittee on Health and Environment and the Education and Labor Subcommittee on Employer-Employee Relations
No further action was ever taken: the bill never received a subcommittee or committee vote and never reached the House floor before the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001

The bill's most contested provision, allowing state-law damage suits against plans and insurers, would have amended ERISA's preemption rules, the mechanism that had shielded managed care plans from most patient lawsuits

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers and HMOs, which kept operating under ERISA's limits on patient lawsuits and without the mandated coverage, review, and disclosure requirements. Patients who faced plan denials kept the pre-1999 rules, with no federal right to external appeal or to sue.

for.name: Rep. Greg Ganske
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and promoted it in repeated floor remarks from February through June 1999

against.name: Rep. Tom Bliley
against.what_they_did: His committee received the bill in February 1999 and never reported it out or scheduled a markup

against.name: Rep. Bill Goodling
against.role: Chair, House Education and the Workforce Committee
against.what_they_did: His committee, which shared jurisdiction over the bill's ERISA provisions, likewise never acted on it

against.name: Health insurance and managed care industry
against.what_they_did: Opposed federal patient-protection mandates and especially the expansion of patient lawsuit rights against plans during the 1999 managed-care debate

sides.party_line_note: The bill drew cosponsors from both parties (14 Republicans, 3 Democrats), but it never received a vote in committee or on the floor, so the record shows no partisan breakdown of support or opposition.

industries.note: The bill would have imposed coverage mandates (emergency, specialists, clinical trials, mastectomy stays), strict utilization-review and external-appeal rules, disclosure requirements, and — most threatening to the industry — a state-law right to sue plans for injuries caused by plan decisions. Insurers' interest in avoiding these rules ran directly against patients' interest in enforceable protections.

Employers would have faced some compliance and premium costs, but the bill deliberately shields employers and plan sponsors from the new state-law damage suits except when the employer itself directly decides a benefits claim and causes injury. Business groups nonetheless generally opposed federal managed-care mandates.

industries.industry: Physicians and other health care providers
industries.note: The bill bans gag clauses, voids contracts that shift plan liability onto doctors, restricts physician incentive plans that reward denials, protects doctors who report quality problems, and requires notice and appeal procedures for being dropped from networks. Providers' interests here line up with patients' interests in candid medical advice.
